clue.text: Secured mobile in deal

indicators.note: Something mobile is free to move around, so the letters it points at are free to move into a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

explanation.surface: A phone contract finally locked in, with a new mobile thrown into the deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' looks like a phone in the surface; here it only says the letters of IN DEAL are free to move.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the informal sense: to nail a deal or a win is to clinch it, make it fast.

clue.text: Write about boxer from mountainous land

indicators.note: To turn about is to face the other way, so the word it follows is written the other way round.

parts.note: to pen = to write
Muhammad Ali, the crossword's favourite boxer

explanation.surface: An instruction to write a profile of a fighter who hails from a mountain country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Write about boxer' reads as a journalist's assignment; 'about' is really turning PEN around. The definition is adjectival: Nepali means from Nepal, the Himalayan land.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: Nepal holds much of the Himalaya, and Nepali is its adjective, so 'from mountainous land' fits.

clue.text: Hurt in martial art, almost holding on

indicators.note: Almost means not quite all of it, so the word loses its last letter.

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: Holding means gripping something within, so the next piece goes inside this one.

parts.note: JUDO without its last letter, which 'almost' asks for
re = on, concerning, as in 'a report on/re the matter'; it goes inside JUD

explanation.surface: Someone got hurt doing a martial art, nearly managing to hang on.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a judo bout gone wrong. RE for 'on' is the memo-heading sense: 'on the subject of'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are past participles meaning harmed in body.

clue.text: Name of woman rising in the morning with me

indicators.note: Rising means going up, and in a down entry going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards.

parts.note: a.m. = in the morning
taken as written, placed 'with' the AM

explanation.surface: A woman who gets up in the morning alongside the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising in the morning' paints someone getting out of bed; in a down clue, rising means read upwards, so AM ME becomes EMMA.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the answer is one particular woman's first name, as in Jane Austen's heroine.

clue.text: Healthcare worker they'd said regularly gets involved in back operation

indicators.note: the picked letters go inside the reversed abbreviation
back says the abbreviation is turned round to read the other way

parts.note: the regular, even-placed letters of they'd said: its second, fourth, sixth and eighth

explanation.surface: A physiotherapist, people said, often helps after back surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back operation' sounds like spinal surgery, which suits the physio, but 'back' turns OP into PO, and the regular letters of 'they'd said' sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Physio is short for physiotherapist, a healthcare professional who treats injuries with exercise and massage.

clue.text: Worker rejected untrustworthy person's support

parts.note: a hand = a worker, as in farmhand

indicators.note: To reject something is to send it back, so the word is sent back to front.

parts.note: a liar cannot be trusted

explanation.surface: An employee turns down the backing of someone they don't trust.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as office politics; 'support' sounds like backing, but it is a physical rail you grip on stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: a handrail is a rail you grip on stairs, there to support you.

clue.text: Lifting, say, is exercise

indicators.note: Lifting means raising, and in a down entry raising letters means reading them from the bottom up, so they reverse.

parts.note: to put = to say, as in 'to put it bluntly'
taken as written

explanation.surface: A claim that lifting weights, for example, counts as exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifting, say' reads as weightlifting given as an example; 'say' is really PUT, and 'Lifting' turns PUT IS upside down in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the sit-up, raising the trunk from lying flat, is one particular exercise for the stomach muscles.

clue.text: On vacation, ordered food of dubious nature

indicators.note: A vacated room has been emptied, so on vacation the word is emptied of its middle, leaving only its outer letters.

parts.note: ORDERED emptied, leaving its outer letters O and D
a dish = an item of food

explanation.surface: A holiday-maker orders a meal abroad and suspects it's not quite right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' reads as a holiday; in crosswords it means a word is vacated, keeping only its outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: oddish means somewhat odd, a little questionable, which is what 'of dubious nature' describes.

clue.text: Finally remedy hole in father's nightwear

indicators.note: In means inside, so the letters before it are placed inside the word after it.

parts.note: pa = father, plus the S; YJAM goes inside it
a hole = a jam, a tight spot, as in 'in a hole'

indicators.note: Finally means at the very end, so take the last letter of the next word.

parts.note: last letter of remedY

explanation.surface: A plea to mend the hole in Dad's pyjamas at last.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is darning, but 'hole' is a predicament, hence JAM. PYJAMAS is the British spelling of pajamas.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: pyjamas are the loose jacket and trousers worn in bed, the commonest nightwear.

clue.text: Some Victorians and all Edwardians in lightweight footwear

indicators.note: Some means a portion of what follows, so the answer is a run of letters taken from inside those words.

parts.note: the run starts at the last letter of Victorians and ends two letters into Edwardians

explanation.surface: A claim about period dress: a few Victorians, and every Edwardian, wore sandals.
explanation.walkthrough: The history-of-fashion surface hides the answer across four words: victorianS AND ALL EDwardians. Sandalled, with the double L, is the British spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: sandals are light open shoes, so someone sandalled is in lightweight footwear.

clue.text: Renowned editor finishing new books

indicators.note: Finishing something means coming at its end, so this piece goes last.

parts.note: n = new
OT = Old Testament, a set of books
ed = editor; it finishes the word

explanation.surface: A famous editor puts the last touches to some new books.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about publishing, so 'books' and 'editor' seem to belong together; here they are separate pieces, and 'finishing' just places ED at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a noted scholar and a renowned scholar are both widely known.

clue.text: Bird left Noah's vessel

parts.note: l = left
the boat Noah built for the flood

explanation.surface: A bird flew off from Noah's ark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as a verb, the bird leaving the ark, which echoes the dove and raven Noah sent out; it is only the letter L.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the lark, famous for singing as it climbs, is one particular bird.

clue.text: Ciphers gent uncovered beside underground chambers

indicators.note: Beside means standing next to, so the two pieces are simply put side by side.

parts.note: gENt without its outer letters
crypts are vaults beneath churches

explanation.surface: A man stripped bare next to some cellars, as if in a spy thriller full of codes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ciphers' looks like a plural noun, codes; it is a verb here, meaning puts into code.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: as verbs, to cipher a message and to encrypt it both mean to put it into code.

clue.text: Insect hidden in ordinary fruit

indicators.note: Something hidden in a place is tucked inside it, so the first piece goes inside the second.

parts.note: plain = ordinary; it is split to hold the insect
the crossword's standard insect; goes inside PLAIN

explanation.surface: A bug is concealed inside an unremarkable piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hidden in' tempts a solver to look for letters running inside 'ordinary fruit'; here it puts ANT inside a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the plantain is a starchy banana-like fruit, usually eaten cooked.

clue.text: Spotted dog close to field barking at animal

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the word whose last letter is taken

indicators.note: barking means mad, so the letters go wild into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A dog near a field barks at some other creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' fits a dog so well that it hides its other sense, mad, which is the anagram signal; barking mad is British slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dalmatian is the dog breed famous for its white coat covered in black or liver spots.

clue.text: Dull Renault hybrid

indicators.note: A hybrid is a cross or mixture, so the letters of the word are mixed up.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: A verdict on a hybrid Renault car: boring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hybrid' reads as a petrol-electric car, which fits Renault, the French carmaker; it is really the mixing signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A near-synonym from colour: neutral shades such as beige and grey are muted, dull.

clue.text: Lightly hit adept shot to gain lead in polo

indicators.note: the jumbled letters take in, or gain, the single letter
shot means ruined or broken, so the letters of adept are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

indicators.note: the lead of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A skilled player takes a gentle swing to get the lead in a polo match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like a polo stroke, but it is the anagram signal on 'adept'.
explanation.definitionFit: To tap is to strike gently, so tapped means hit lightly.

clue.text: Just married before end of financial year

parts.note: m = married, as in genealogies
ere = before, poetically

indicators.note: The end of a word is its final letter, so take only that.

parts.note: last letter of financiaL
y = year

explanation.surface: A couple wed just before the tax year closes, perhaps for the tax break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of financial year' reads as one accounting phrase; 'end of' takes only the L, and 'year' is a separate Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'just a child' and 'merely a child' both mean only, no more than.

clue.text: Dispatched parts competently, without thinking

indicators.note: To part something is to split it open, as a curtain parts, so the other piece goes into the gap.

parts.note: ably = competently; it is split to hold SENT
sent = dispatched; goes inside ABLY

explanation.surface: Someone shipped out machine parts efficiently but mindlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' reads as a noun, spare parts in a warehouse; it is a verb, SENT parting ABLY.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiomatic synonym: doing something absently means your mind is absent, so you do it without thinking.

clue.text: Blemish on female's neck covering

indicators.note: In a down entry, one thing on another sits above it, so the first piece comes before the second.

parts.note: a scar is a mark on the skin
f = female; the ’s just makes the surface read

explanation.surface: A woman has a mark on her neck, which she covers up.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a scar on a woman's neck; the break falls after 'female’s', which is just F. A scarf is exactly what might cover a scar there.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: a scarf is a strip of cloth wrapped around the neck, covering it.

clue.text: Nobleman appointed to host king

indicators.note: A host takes guests into their home, so this word takes the next piece inside it.

parts.note: due = appointed, as in 'at the due time'
K = king, as in chess; goes inside DUE

explanation.surface: A lord is designated to entertain the king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appointed' seems to be about a nobleman's role; it gives DUE, as in the appointed or due hour.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: in the British peerage the duke is the highest rank of nobleman.

clue.text: Finished deliveries

definitions.note: 'Deliveries' is plural because the answer is a set of six balls.
definitions.meaning: the sense of done, ended: 'the game is finished'
cricket: a delivery is one ball bowled, and the answer is a set of six of them

explanation.surface: The deliveries are finished; the parcels have all gone out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliveries' reads as parcels; in cricket, a delivery is one ball bowled, and six of them make an over.
explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: 'it's over' means finished, and in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled.

clue.text: Public square is place jazzman used now and again

parts.note: Pl. is the street-name abbreviation for Place

indicators.note: Used now and again means used only some of the time, at intervals, so take every other letter.

parts.note: every second letter of jAzZmAn

explanation.surface: A town square is where a jazz musician plays from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a busker in a square; 'place' looks like a synonym for square but is the address abbreviation PL.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym borrowed from Spanish: a plaza is an open square in a town, used by the public.

clue.text: Five soldiers in gamble split up

indicators.note: In means inside, so the pieces before it go inside the word after it.

parts.note: to dice = to gamble; it is split to hold V and OR
V = five in Roman numerals
OR = other ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Five soldiers gambling together fall out and go their separate ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split up' sounds like the soldiers scattering; it is the definition, a verb for ending a marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiomatic synonym: couples who split up have separated, and divorcing is the legal form of it.

clue.text: Clearly describe part of fish seen in Scottish river

indicators.note: Something seen in a river is inside it, so this piece goes inside the river's name.

parts.note: the Dee flows through Aberdeenshire to Aberdeen
a fin is part of a fish; goes inside the river

explanation.surface: A request to describe clearly the bit of a fish spotted in a Scottish river.
explanation.walkthrough: The angling surface hides the definition at the front, where 'Clearly describe' looks like an instruction to the solver; the Dee is a common crossword river.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to define is to set out exactly what something is, which is describing it clearly.

clue.text: Ruffled young mare carrying queen

indicators.note: A horse carrying a rider holds her on its back, so this word holds the next piece inside it.

parts.note: a filly is a young female horse; it holds R
R = Regina, Latin for queen; goes inside FILLY

explanation.surface: A flustered young horse gives the queen a ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruffled' looks like the mare's mood, flustered; it means trimmed with ruffles.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in dressmaking: ruffles and frills are the same gathered trim, so ruffled cloth is frilly.
